questions.text: Two balls roll across the floor. The ball that is moving FASTER has what?
questions.explanation: The faster an object moves, the more energy of motion (kinetic energy) it has. A faster ball can push harder when it hits something.

questions.text: Energy can be moved from place to place by which of these?
options: Sound, light, heat, and electric currents
questions.explanation: Energy can be transferred by sound, by light, by heat, and by electric currents. All of these can carry energy from one place to another.

questions.text: When one moving marble hits another marble, what happens to the energy?
options: It is transferred from one marble to the other
questions.explanation: In a collision, energy is transferred from the moving marble to the one it hits, which is why the second marble starts to move.

questions.text: A toaster changes electrical energy into which forms of energy?
questions.explanation: A toaster changes electrical energy into heat (to toast the bread) and light (the wires glow). It converts one form of energy into others.

questions.text: A wave with a taller height, called a bigger amplitude, carries what?
questions.explanation: A wave with a bigger amplitude (taller height) carries more energy. A large ocean wave has more energy than a small ripple.

questions.text: The distance from the top of one wave to the top of the next wave is called the what?
questions.explanation: The distance between two wave crests (tops) is called the wavelength.

questions.text: Why are you able to see a book on a table?
options: Light reflects off the book into your eyes
Books always glow on their own
questions.explanation: You see the book because light bounces (reflects) off it and travels into your eyes. Your eyes do not send out light.

questions.text: Which of these sends information using a pattern?
options: Flashing a light in Morse code
questions.explanation: Flashing a light in Morse code uses a pattern of long and short flashes to send information. Patterns can carry messages.

questions.text: A cactus has a thick, waxy stem. How does this structure help the cactus?
options: It helps the cactus store water in the desert
questions.explanation: The thick, waxy stem helps the cactus store water and keep it from drying out, which lets the cactus survive in the dry desert.

questions.text: What is the main job of a plant's roots?
options: Take in water and hold the plant in place
questions.explanation: Roots take in water and minerals from the soil and anchor the plant so it does not fall over. Leaves, not roots, catch sunlight.

questions.text: When you touch something hot, your senses quickly send information to your what?
questions.explanation: Sense receptors in your skin send signals to your brain, which processes the information and makes you pull your hand away.

questions.text: What can fossils found in rock tell scientists about?
questions.explanation: Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of living things. They give scientists clues about plants and animals that lived long ago.

questions.text: In rock layers that have not been disturbed, where is the OLDEST layer usually found?
questions.explanation: In undisturbed rock layers, the oldest layer is at the bottom because it was laid down first. Newer layers pile on top of it.

questions.text: Which process slowly breaks rock into smaller and smaller pieces?
questions.explanation: Weathering slowly breaks rock into smaller pieces over time, for example when water freezes in cracks or wind wears the rock down.

questions.text: When moving water carries away soil and small rocks, this is called what?
questions.explanation: Erosion is the moving of weathered soil and rock from one place to another, often by water or wind.

questions.text: Which kind of map shows the height of mountains and the depth of valleys?
questions.explanation: A topographic map uses lines to show the shape of the land, including how high mountains are and how deep valleys go.

questions.text: Which of these is a nonrenewable energy source, meaning it can run out?
questions.explanation: Coal is a nonrenewable resource. Once it is used up, it takes millions of years to form again. Sunlight, wind, and flowing water are renewable.

questions.text: Which choice would best help protect a building from earthquake damage?
questions.explanation: Flexible, reinforced structures can sway without breaking during an earthquake, which helps protect the building and the people inside.

questions.text: A well-defined engineering problem includes what?
options: Clear goals for success and limits called constraints
questions.explanation: Engineers define a problem with criteria (what success looks like) and constraints (the limits, such as cost or materials). These guide the design.

questions.text: After testing a design, how should an engineer improve it?
options: Use the test results to make the design better
Throw the design away without looking
questions.explanation: Engineers use what they learn from testing to improve the design. Fair tests show which parts work and which parts need to be fixed.
